cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable (cross-sectional two-round interviewing): Interviews took place in May 2016 and July 2016 (55 total participants; 36 in the second 60-minute round, PDF p. 8), but the paper does not clarify whether Round 2 re-interviewed a subset of Round 1 respondents (implying 19 non-continuers) or sampled 19 exploratory and 36 in-depth participants independently.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable as causal confounding (qualitative phenomenological study), with moderate contextual limitation: The study does not estimate causal treatment effects, instead constructing a narrative fabula. Although the authors argue chronic water scarcity in Kathmandu holds issue salience constant (PDF p. 4), thematic narratives are not stratified by household income, caste/ethnicity, land tenure, or piped-network access—factors that shape coping capacity and willingness to protest.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak (secondary contextual description only): Legal, regulatory, and institutional features—such as the 2008 PPP appointment of Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited (KUKL), Melamchi Water Supply Project contract delays, cash-based informal tanker transactions without written contracts, and the absence of legal mechanisms regulating vendor water price, quantity, or quality (PDF pp. 3, 7, 14)—are cited from secondary sources as background context rather than measured or coded from primary legal instruments.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Lived experiences were elicited through two iterative interview rounds totaling 40 hours of audio recordings, transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo (PDF pp. 8-9). However, the interview schedule/prompts are not provided, the interview language(s) and translation quality-assurance procedures are unreported despite hermeneutic reliance on wording, and interviewer positionality is unaddressed.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for subjective lived-experience perceptions, weak for objective water/coping outcomes: Water supply intermittency, household coping expenditures, emotional distress, and institutional distrust are captured solely via unverified self-reported interview narratives (PDF pp. 8-13), without household water testing, utility supply logs, or structured expenditure verification; claims that residents 'over-estimate' resilience therefore depend on contrasting subjective quotes against secondary economic studies rather than paired household measurements.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern (no pre-registered qualitative protocol): While no study protocol is cited and there is a minor inconsistency between the text referencing 'three main themes' (PDF p. 9) and Tables 2-3 displaying five units of meaning and six main-theme labels (PDF pp. 9-13), transparency is strengthened by full reporting of statement frequencies across all five units (Table 2) and a four-page matrix of verbatim meaning units, condensations, sub-themes, and themes covering both passive coping and active dissatisfaction (Table 3).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High / Moderate-to-high concern (Can't tell recruitment procedure): Although respondent demographics are summarized (55 participants overall; 36 in Round 2, mean age 41, range 26-75, 36% female, spanning students, housewives, professionals, government servants, business owners, and retirees, PDF p. 8), the paper omits sampling strategy, neighborhood/ward selection (piped vs. unpiped peri-urban zones), inclusion/exclusion criteria, and refusal rates, and women—typically primary household water managers—made up only 36% of Round 2 interviewees.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors clearly state their research aim: to investigate the 'paradox of social resilience' amid chronic water scarcity and delayed municipal infrastructure (Melamchi Water Supply Project / KUKL) in the Kathmandu Valley by constructing a narrative 'fabula' from residents' lived experiences and evaluating two hypotheses—emotional numbing (H1) and rational calculus of trade-offs (H2)—and their potential integration.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF pp. 3-4); Methods (PDF p. 8)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative phenomenological approach is well suited to the study's focus on subjective lived experiences, emotional and cognitive coping processes, and shared narrative structures underlying public quiescence toward water insecurity—dimensions the authors persuasively argue are missed by purely quantitative economic valuation studies.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF p. 4); Coping costs and the paradox of social resilience (PDF p. 5); Methods (PDF p. 8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify combining a phenomenological hermeneutical lived-experience design (citing van Manen 1984; Sadala & Adorno 2002; Lindseth & Norberg 2004) with Bal's (2009) narratological 'fabula' framework to trace how events, actors, time, and location structure residents' perceptions of coping, while explicitly acknowledging phenomenological limitations regarding subjectivity and non-replicability.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While sample sizes and basic demographics are reported (55 total participants; 36 in Round 2 with mean age 41, range 26-75, 36% female, across diverse occupations), the paper gives no account of how participants were identified, approached, or sampled (e.g., purposive, snowball, or street convenience), which neighborhoods or water-service zones of Kathmandu were included, whether Round 2 participants overlapped with Round 1, or whether any approached residents declined.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection followed a coherent two-stage interview process in Kathmandu: exploratory 15-30 minute interviews on 26 May 2016 informed a detailed set of questions administered in July 2016 to 36 residents (averaging 60 minutes per interview), producing 40 hours of audio tape that were transcribed and translated. However, specific interview prompts, interview settings, source language/translation verification, and data saturation criteria are not reported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: There is no reflexive discussion of the researchers' role, outsider institutional positionality (Singapore-based authors researching Kathmandu residents), who conducted and translated the fieldwork, or how researcher assumptions influenced interview interactions and the 'naive understanding' phase of hermeneutic coding; the researcher-participant relationship is mentioned only generically in the closing sentence of the paper as a broad virtue of phenomenology.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Although interview excerpts in Table 3 are presented without personal identifiers, the paper contains no mention of institutional ethics/IRB review, how the study was explained to participants, informed consent procedures (including consent to 40 hours of audio recording), or data confidentiality safeguards.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors apply Lindseth & Norberg's (2004) phenomenological hermeneutical method using NVivo, detailing iterative reading for 'naive understanding', extraction of 228 thematic statements across five units of meaning (Table 2), and condensation into sub-themes and main themes transparently displayed across four pages of verbatim meaning units (Table 3), while engaging competing narrative strands (resignation vs. anger). Rigor is somewhat tempered by unreported coder numbers/consensus checks, unverified translation fidelity, and a minor discrepancy between the text citing 'three main themes' and Tables 2-3 listing five units of meaning / six main-theme labels.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods (PDF p. 9); Results and discussion, Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 9-14)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly articulated and explicitly evaluated against H1 (emotional numbing / 'Hero Hypothesis') and H2 (rational calculus of trade-offs), synthesized into a three-element fabula and causal loop diagram (Figure 1), and contextualized with policy implications, though respondent validation (member checking) was not performed and inferences of 'over-estimated' resilience rely partly on external secondary benchmarks.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results and discussion, Figure 1 (PDF pp. 9, 14-16); Conclusions (PDF pp. 16-17)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment — Valuable conceptual and policy contribution with constrained transferability: The study advances water governance and socio-ecological resilience scholarship by demonstrating how passive everyday coping (informal tanker/bottled water reliance) and acute institutional distrust coexist in a tenuous equilibrium that masks vulnerability and delays collective pressure on failing public utilities. Transferability is constrained, as the authors acknowledge, by the non-replicability of phenomenology and the uncharacterized sampling frame within Kathmandu.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable conceptual and policy contribution (with transferability constrained by opaque sampling and absent reflexivity)
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods (PDF p. 8); Results and discussion (PDF pp. 14-16); Conclusions (PDF pp. 16-17)

overall_narrative_summary: Ching et al. (2019) conduct a primary qualitative phenomenological hermeneutical study examining why Kathmandu Valley residents absorb substantial economic and emotional coping costs from chronic water scarcity and repeated delays in the Melamchi Water Supply Project without mounting sustained public protest. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits clear aims (Q1: Yes), a well-justified qualitative phenomenological and narratological ('fabula') design (Q2: Yes; Q3: Yes), substantial two-round interview data totaling 40 hours of transcribed and translated audio from up to 55/36 residents (Q5: Yes), a transparent quote-to-theme hermeneutic condensation matrix in NVivo (Q8: Yes, albeit without multi-coder verification details and with a minor theme-numbering discrepancy between text and tables), and a coherent synthesis linking passive coping and institutional distrust via a causal loop model (Q9: Yes; Q10: Valuable conceptual contribution). Overall methodological concern is Moderate (1 No and 2 Can't tell items across Q1-Q9), driven by three core omissions: (1) complete absence of recruitment/sampling details, spatial coverage across piped vs. unpiped areas, and non-response information, alongside male over-representation (64% male in Round 2) (Q4: Can't tell); (2) absence of researcher reflexivity regarding foreign researcher positionality, field interviewer identity, and cross-language translation dynamics (Q6: No); and (3) no reporting of ethics committee approval or informed consent procedures (Q7: Can't tell). Legal and regulatory dimensions of municipal utility governance and informal water markets are treated purely as secondary background context rather than empirically measured legal variables.
overall_rating: Moderate concern (2 Can't tell and 1 No items)
study_design_identified: Primary qualitative study (phenomenological hermeneutical interview study / lived experiences narrative analysis)
where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction & conceptual background (PDF pp. 1-6); Kathmandu case background (PDF pp. 6-8); Methods (PDF pp. 8-9); Results and discussion including Tables 2-3 and Figure 1 (PDF pp. 9-16); Conclusions (PDF pp. 16-17).
why_tool_chosen: The empirical component of the paper is an exclusively qualitative phenomenological hermeneutical interview study ('lived experiences approach') of Kathmandu residents (55 total participants across two interview rounds; 36 one-hour Round 2 interviews transcribed, translated, and thematically coded in NVivo following Lindseth & Norberg 2004). Statement counts in Table 2 simply report qualitative coding frequencies across themes rather than a quantitative survey or statistical design (ruling out MMAT and JBI checklists), there is no intervention comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I), and legal/institutional aspects of water governance are discussed only as secondary background context (making CASP Qualitative Checklist the exact matching primary qualitative tool).
